description:
Farm Titans 🌾🛰️ | Field Shift
We’re building a crop-rotation tool that turns NASA satellite data into clear, explainable advice farmers can use: protecting soil, saving water and adapting to a changing climate. We bring AI engineering, full-stack development and modern UX, and we aim to ship a polished, working product. Drought is already hurting Romanian farms, and we want to build something that outlives the weekend. Team complete, but happy to swap ideas!
summary:
Field Signal helps a farmer test a crop rotation before planting. In 2025, maize in Alba County, Romania, came in 42% below its long-term trend, and farmers had to choose the next crop with no way to see how it would have coped.

Our web app lets a farmer tap their parcel on a map and compare rotations. It combines NASA POWER weather, SMAP soil moisture and satellite greenness with soil and crop maps. We trained our own models on this data: a field model that learned from more than 300,000 fields in 7 countries how crops respond to weather, and yield models for seven crops. They replay past seasons on the farmer's field for each crop, and every rotation gets a score out of 100. A second view shows feed buyers where crops such as maize are at risk of a bad year.

This addresses the Field Shift challenge by turning free NASA data into a decision one farmer can act on, from a phone, in Romanian or English. It matters because a rotation is a bet placed months ahead, and a bad one costs a whole season. Field Signal is live at https://fieldsignal.land.
details:
What does it do?

Field Signal answers one question for a farmer: "What should I plant next on this field?" The farmer taps their parcel on a satellite map (all 171,607 declared parcels in Alba County, Romania are loaded), enters the current rotation and sets priorities: yield, water, soil, risk. The app compares the current rotation with the best alternatives and gives each a score out of 100. It also replays every season from 2001 to 2025 to show how each rotation would have done in the good years and the bad ones.

For a whole farm, the farmer imports their parcels and gets a plan: how many hectares of each crop go on each field, inside EU farm-subsidy rules, with a checklist for the yearly declaration.

A second view serves feed buyers. It shows a two-year yield outlook by region and crop, and how many days of stock a feed mill has before it must buy.

How does it work?

We built a slim, LSTM-based world model for a field. It predicts a field’s greenness and soil moisture for the next month from their current values, conditioned on the weather and on the crop history: this year’s crop and the two before it. A three-year autoregressive rollout simulates full seasons before they happen.

Training covered 306,373 sample points in 7 countries, Romania and its neighbours, with greenness from NASA HLS, soil moisture from SMAP and weather from NASA POWER across 2016–2024. We tested on 39,588 points in eleven regions the model had never seen. Over a three-year rollout from September 2021, running on its own predictions, monthly R² was 0.65 to 0.69 for greenness and 0.84 to 0.88 for soil moisture. A four-year rollout held the same level. We trained five seeds to help measure uncertainty.

The crop is an input, so we can move it. Weather stays observed, the crop changes, and the model plays the year out again. We checked these simulated seasons against fields that really grew the swapped-in crop under the same weather: mean greenness error was 0.02 to 0.04, and the peak month was right for all six crops. When a farmer asks “what if I planted sunflower here instead,” the answer is a simulated season. It reflects what happened on fields where farmers made that choice.

A rule-based layer turns the simulations into a plan. It first prunes rotations that break agronomic rules and specific EU regulations. Each remaining rotation is rolled out under past weather periods and scored on yield, water, soil health and risk. The farmer’s priorities weight the scores, and a risk setting decides how much the worst weather period counts against the average.

Seven XGBoost regressors, one per crop, read a season’s peak and integrated greenness and return tonnes per hectare. They train on Eurostat NUTS 2 yield, production over area, centred on each region’s own mean and scored leave-one-year-out against that mean. Applied to the world model’s simulated seasons, they give each region’s expected yield per crop, which feeds the supply view.

Benefits and intended impact

A rotation is a bet placed months before the weather is known. In 2025, maize in Alba came in 42% below its long-term trend. Field Signal lets a farmer test that bet against 25 real seasons before buying seed, on a phone, in Romanian or English. Feed buyers see early where supply is at risk, so they can contract earlier or support farmers who add peas or soybean.

How is it creative?

We do not try to forecast next year's weather. We replay the past: the same field, the real weather of each past year, a different crop. A farmer already remembers those years, so the result is easy to check against experience.

What we considered

- Trust: the model is tested on regions it never saw, and we say where it is weak (barley and dry pulses yields are rough).

- Honesty: the tool supports the farmer's judgment and does not replace it. It cannot see hail, pests, prices or management.

- Access: mobile first, plain language, two languages, open data only.

- No NASA logos and no implied endorsement.

Tools

- Web: TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL, three.js.

- API: Python, FastAPI, OR-Tools, PostgreSQL.

- Models and data: PyTorch, XGBoost, NumPy, Polars, Google Earth Engine.

- Hosting: Azure Container Apps, GitHub Actions.

- In-app assistant: an existing open language model (Qwen), which explains results; we did not train it.
